label: Faction military power
summary: The game concept Faction Military Power: a faction's total military strength compared with its target's.
details: In a text, `[faction_military_power|E]` shows "Faction Military Power" linked to the concept's explanation. Each member adds their full strength while in the faction; when the target is a member's liege, the member's strength is also taken off the target's side.

label: Faction
summary: Another name of the game concept Faction, in the plural: groups of vassals with shared political aims.
details: In a text, `[factions|E]` shows "Factions" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts.

label: Faith
summary: The game concept Faith: a particular branch of a larger religion, which every character and county follows, like a culture.
details: In a text, `[faith|E]` shows "Faith" linked to the concept's explanation. A faith's beliefs are set by the tenets and doctrines of its main rite; other rites can differ from it. Vanilla uses it in a great many texts.

label: Astray
summary: The game concept Astray: a hostility level between faiths, for a rite that differs only in minor ways.
details: In a text, `[faith_astray|E]` shows "Astray" linked to the concept's explanation. Marriage between the two can still happen. It is one of the levels of faith hostility, between Righteous and Hostile.

label: Evil
summary: The game concept Evil: the highest hostility level between faiths, for a rite seen as abhorrent.
details: In a text, `[faith_evil|E]` shows "Evil" linked to the concept's explanation. Marriage between the two is rare, and holy wars can be fought.

label: Hostile
summary: The game concept Hostile: a hostility level between faiths, for a rite that differs a great deal.
details: In a text, `[faith_hostile|E]` shows "Hostile" linked to the concept's explanation. Marriage between the two can still happen, and holy wars can be fought.

label: Faith hostility
summary: The game concept Faith Hostility: how faiths and rites stand towards each other, set by how closely related they are.
details: In a text, `[faith_hostility|E]` shows "Faith Hostility" linked to the concept's explanation. Closeness depends on such things as a shared religion or religious family and special doctrines; faiths far apart can often fight holy wars against each other.

label: Righteous
summary: The game concept Righteous: the friendliest hostility level between faiths, for a rite seen as legitimate.
details: In a text, `[faith_righteous|E]` shows "Righteous" linked to the concept's explanation. Marriage between the two is common.

label: Faith
summary: Another name of the game concept Faith, in the possessive form "Faith's".
details: In a text, `[faithpossessive|E]` shows "Faith's" linked to the explanation of faith (a branch of a larger religion that every character and county follows).

label: Faith
summary: Another name of the game concept Faith, in the plural: branches of larger religions.
details: In a text, `[faiths|E]` shows "Faiths" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in many texts.

label: Fallback heir
summary: The game concept Fallback Heir: the character who becomes heir to a title when its regular line of succession is empty.
details: In a text, `[fallback_heir|E]` shows "Fallback Heir" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Fallback heir title
summary: The game concept Fallback Heir Title: a title whose holder becomes heir to another title when that title's regular line of succession is empty.
details: In a text, `[fallback_heir_title|E]` shows "Fallback Heir Title" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Fame trait
summary: The game concept Fame Trait: a special trait gained in particular circumstances that changes how others regard the character.
details: In a text, `[fame_trait|E]` shows "Fame Trait" linked to the concept's explanation. Such traits come from good deeds, from dark secrets being exposed, or from the circumstances of one's birth.

label: Fame trait
summary: Another name of the game concept Fame Trait, in the plural: special traits that change how others regard a character.
details: In a text, `[fame_traits|E]` shows "Fame Traits" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Artifact rarity
summary: Another name of the game concept Artifact Rarity: the rarity level "Famed", the second highest after Illustrious.
details: In a text, `[famed|E]` shows "Famed" linked to the explanation of artifact rarity. The levels from lowest are Common, Masterwork, Famed and Illustrious. Vanilla uses it in artifact texts, for example "Must be at least Famed".

label: Family
summary: The game concept Family: a character's close family together with their extended family.
details: In a text, `[family|E]` shows "Family" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Powerful family attribute
summary: Another name of the game concept Powerful Family Attribute: a set of bonuses tied to a house in a bureaucratic realm, for the house's members and their liege.
details: In a text, `[family_attribute|E]` shows "Family Attribute" linked to the concept's explanation. It only works while the house counts as a powerful family. Vanilla uses it in administrative texts that name a house's attribute.

label: Estate
summary: Another name of the game concept Estate: a noble family's estate, its private landholding in an administrative realm.
details: In a text, `[family_estate|E]` shows "Family Estate" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Estate
summary: Another name of the game concept Estate, in the plural: noble families' estates.
details: In a text, `[family_estates|E]` shows "Family Estates" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Japanese manor
summary: Another name of the game concept Japanese Manor: a domicile held by the house head of a notable noble family in Japanese administrative or feudal realms, a private landholding not tied to a landed title.
details: In a text, `[family_manor|E]` shows "Family Manor" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Japanese manor
summary: Another name of the game concept Japanese Manor, in the plural: noble families' manors in Japanese realms.
details: In a text, `[family_manors|E]` shows "Family Manors" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: East Asian mansion
summary: Another name of the game concept East Asian Mansion: a domicile held by the house head of a notable noble family, a private landholding not tied to a landed title.
details: In a text, `[family_mansion|E]` shows "Family Mansion" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: East Asian mansion
summary: Another name of the game concept East Asian Mansion, in the plural: noble families' mansions.
details: In a text, `[family_mansions|E]` shows "Family Mansions" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Family
summary: Another name of the game concept Family: one member of a character's close or extended family.
details: In a text, `[family_member|E]` shows "Family Member" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in kinslayer and AI reason texts.

label: Family
summary: Another name of the game concept Family: the members of a character's close and extended family.
details: In a text, `[family_members|E]` shows "Family Members" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Cultural fascination
summary: Another name of the game concept Cultural Fascination: the one innovation a culture is fascinated by, which it discovers much faster.
details: In a text, `[fascination|E]` shows "Fascination" linked to the concept's explanation. How fast depends on the culture head's skills; each innovation uses a particular skill. The culture head can change the fascination freely. Vanilla uses it in message and tribute mission texts.

label: Fatalities
summary: The game concept Fatalities: characters who died as a direct result of a plague or a natural disaster.
details: In a text, `[fatalities|E]` shows "Fatalities" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Favor
summary: The game concept Favor: a debt one character owes another, a kind of hook.
details: In a text, `[favor|E]` shows "Favor" linked to the concept's explanation. Favors come about in many ways, often through events; every child born to a noble house owes its house head one favor from the start.

label: Favored era
summary: The game concept Favored Era: the Son of Heaven's declared will of Heaven for the dynastic cycle, which decides which stable era follows once the unstable one ends.
details: In a text, `[favored_era|E]` shows "Favored Era" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Favored era
summary: Another name of the game concept Favored Era, in the possessive form "Favored Era's".
details: In a text, `[favored_era_possessive|E]` shows "Favored Era's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Favored movement
summary: The game concept Favored Movement: the movement that has won the support of the Son of Heaven.
details: In a text, `[favored_movement|E]` shows "Favored Movement" linked to the concept's explanation. Its members get higher candidate scores for titles, among other benefits the concept lists.

label: Favored movement
summary: Another name of the game concept Favored Movement, in the possessive form "Favored Movement's".
details: In a text, `[favored_movement_possessive|E]` shows "Favored Movement's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Favored movement
summary: Another name of the game concept Favored Movement, in the short form "Favored".
details: In a text, `[favored_movement_short|E]` shows "Favored" linked to the explanation of the movement the Son of Heaven supports.

label: Favorite child
summary: The game concept Favorite Child: a direct descendant of the same dynasty whom a player ruler chooses to favor.
details: In a text, `[favorite_child|E]` shows "Favorite Child" linked to the concept's explanation. The favorite child has a better opinion of the ruler, and when the ruler dies the player can go on as them instead of the heir. Children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren can be chosen.

label: Favor
summary: Another name of the game concept Favor, in the plural: debts characters owe each other, a kind of hook.
details: In a text, `[favors|E]` shows "Favors" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Feast
summary: The game concept Feast: an activity where the rulers and courtiers of a realm come together to celebrate.
details: In a text, `[feast|E]` shows "Feast" linked to the concept's explanation. Guests lose stress and think better of the host, and other things can happen when so many people meet. A ruler invites their liege and their vassals, among others.

label: Fertility
summary: The game concept Fertility: how able a character is to have children.
details: In a text, `[fertility|E]` shows "Fertility" linked to the concept's explanation. This is a character's fertility, not a county's (that is county fertility). Vanilla uses it in vow, trait and core texts.

label: Fertility equilibrium
summary: The game concept Fertility Equilibrium: the level a county's fertility moves towards over time.
details: In a text, `[fertility_equilibrium|E]` shows "Fertility Equilibrium" linked to the concept's explanation. The county's fertility grows while below it and falls while above it; the level and the speed of change depend mostly on the county's growth and consumption modifiers.

label: Fervor
summary: The game concept Fervor: a faith's spiritual unity, from 0 to 100%.
details: In a text, `[fervor|E]` shows "Fervor" linked to the concept's explanation. It rises through aggressive expansion (converting counties, winning holy wars, fending off holy wars) and falls when the faith splinters, for example through very divergent rites.

label: Fervor
summary: Another name of the game concept Fervor: it shows the fervor icon instead of a word.
details: The game's text for this name is the fervor icon (`@fervor_icon!`), so `[fervor_i]` in a text shows that icon. Vanilla puts it before fervor values, as in the texts for fervor going up or down.

label: Feudal
summary: The game concept Feudal: the government form in which a liege gives vassals land to rule in return for levies and taxes.
details: In a text, `[feudal|E]` shows "Feudal" linked to the concept's explanation. What each vassal owes is set by their own vassal contract with the liege.

label: Feudal
summary: Another name of the game concept Feudal: the feudal government, where a liege gives vassals land in return for levies and taxes.
details: In a text, `[feudal_government|E]` shows "Feudal Government" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Feudal
summary: Another name of the game concept Feudal: it shows the feudal government icon instead of a word.
details: The game's text for this name is the feudal government icon (`@government_type_feudal!`), so `[feudal_i|E]` shows that icon linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla puts it before feudal opinion modifiers.

label: Feudal
summary: Another name of the game concept Feudal, as "Feudalism": the system where a liege gives vassals land in return for levies and taxes.
details: In a text, `[feudalism|E]` shows "Feudalism" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Secular obligations
summary: Another name of the game concept Secular Obligations: "Fixed Obligations", one of the ways of deciding how much church holding income goes to the local secular ruler.
details: In a text, `[fixed_obligations|E]` shows "Fixed Obligations" linked to the explanation of secular obligations. Vanilla uses it in the Christian church situation texts.

label: Fleet
summary: The game concept Fleet: the ships an army boards automatically when it moves into a sea zone.
details: In a text, `[fleet|E]` shows "Fleet" linked to the concept's explanation. Embarking costs gold, for getting the ships. At sea an army moves fast but costs 25% more upkeep.

label: Fleet
summary: Another name of the game concept Fleet, in the plural: the ships armies board in sea zones.
details: In a text, `[fleets|E]` shows "Fleets" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Flood
summary: The game concept Flood: a natural disaster that does growing damage across many counties along the banks of major rivers.
details: In a text, `[flood|E]` shows "Flood" linked to the concept's explanation. Floods only happen along major rivers.

label: Flood
summary: Another name of the game concept Flood, as "Flooded": struck by a flood.
details: In a text, `[flooded|E]` shows "Flooded" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Flood
summary: Another name of the game concept Flood, in the plural: floods along major rivers.
details: In a text, `[floods|E]` shows "Floods" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Raid for captives
summary: The game concept Raid for Captives: a special war started by a ruler whose faith practices human sacrifice, fought to take prisoners for sacrifice.
details: In a text, `[flowery_war|E]` shows "Raid for Captives" linked to the concept's explanation. Either side can win through battles alone, without sieges, by earning enough war score.

label: Raid for captives
summary: Another name of the game concept Raid for Captives, as "Raiding for Captives".
details: In a text, `[flowery_warring|E]` shows "Raiding for Captives" linked to the explanation of this war for taking sacrifice prisoners. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Raid for captives
summary: Another name of the game concept Raid for Captives, in the plural "Raids for Captives".
details: In a text, `[flowery_wars|E]` shows "Raids for Captives" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Focus
summary: The game concept Focus: one of the options within a lifestyle, one of which must be picked when choosing the lifestyle.
details: In a text, `[focus|E]` shows "Focus" linked to the concept's explanation. A focus gives passive bonuses and changes which events appear.

label: Focus
summary: Another name of the game concept Focus, in the plural: the options within a lifestyle.
details: In a text, `[focuses|E]` shows "Focuses" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Follower
summary: The game concept Follower: an unlanded character who travels with an adventurer.
details: In a text, `[follower|E]` shows "Follower" linked to the concept's explanation. In game terms followers are like courtiers, but feel less bound to show respect or stay if they dislike their leader; their opinion together affects the leader.

label: Follower
summary: Another name of the game concept Follower, in the plural: the unlanded characters who travel with an adventurer.
details: In a text, `[followers|E]` shows "Followers" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Follower
summary: Another name of the game concept Follower, as "Following": an adventurer's followers as a whole.
details: In a text, `[following|E]` shows "Following" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in a tutorial text about adventurers.

label: Release your anger interaction
summary: The game concept Release your Anger Interaction: an interaction that lets a stressed character challenge anyone to single combat.
details: In a text, `[force_duel_anyone_interaction|E]` shows "Release your Anger Interaction" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Punish criminal interaction
summary: The game concept Punish Criminal Interaction: an interaction that lets a stressed character challenge criminals to single combat.
details: In a text, `[force_duel_criminals_interaction|E]` shows "Punish Criminal Interaction" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Foreign affairs
summary: The game concept Foreign Affairs: the chancellor's councillor task that improves how other rulers see the character.
details: In a text, `[foreign_affairs|E]` shows "Foreign Affairs" linked to the concept's explanation. For an independent ruler it raises other independent rulers' opinion of them; for a vassal it raises the opinion of the other vassals of the same liege.

label: Fort level
summary: The game concept Fort Level: the strength rating of a fortified holding, which sets how long a siege of it can be expected to last.
details: In a text, `[fort_level|E]` shows "Fort Level" linked to the concept's explanation. Fortified holdings must be besieged and occupied to gain control of the county, and a high fort level needs siege weapons.

label: Fort level
summary: Another name of the game concept Fort Level: it shows the fort icon instead of a word.
details: The game's text for this name is the fort icon (`@fort_icon!`), so `[fort_level_i]` in a text shows that icon. Vanilla puts it before fort level values in tradition texts.

label: Fortification building
summary: The game concept Fortification Building: a building whose main purpose is to raise its holding's fort level or give defenders an advantage.
details: In a text, `[fortification_building|E]` shows "Fortification Building" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Fortification building
summary: Another name of the game concept Fortification Building, in the plural: buildings that raise fort level or help defenders.
details: In a text, `[fortification_buildings|E]` shows "Fortification Buildings" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Fortified holding
summary: The game concept Fortified Holding: a holding with buildings that give it a fort level; county capitals are always fortified.
details: In a text, `[fortified_holding|E]` shows "Fortified Holding" linked to the concept's explanation. To occupy a county fully, all its fortified holdings must be occupied.

label: Fortified holding
summary: Another name of the game concept Fortified Holding, in the plural: holdings with a fort level.
details: In a text, `[fortified_holdings|E]` shows "Fortified Holdings" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Demand submission
summary: The game concept Demand Submission: an interaction that demands a character's loyalty in the form of a hook, using piety, guile or intimidation.
details: In a text, `[fp3_demand_submission_interaction|E]` shows "Demand Submission" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Embellish capital decision
summary: The game concept Embellish Capital Decision: a decision that improves your capital at the expense of a county you conquered recently.
details: In a text, `[fp3_embellish_capital_decision|E]` shows "Embellish Capital Decision" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Rescue house members
summary: The game concept Rescue House Members: a casus belli for house heads that forces the target to free every imprisoned member of the house.
details: In a text, `[fp3_free_house_member_cb|E]` shows "Rescue House Members" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Install a supporter
summary: The game concept Install a Supporter: a war to put a supporter of the Caliphate (a character with that struggle trait) at the head of the target realm.
details: In a text, `[fp3_install_loyalist_cb|E]` shows "Install a Supporter" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Request honorary title
summary: The game concept Request Honorary Title: an interaction that asks your head of faith to honor you with a particular title.
details: In a text, `[fp3_request_honorary_titles_interaction|E]` shows "Request Honorary Title" linked to the concept's explanation. The concept's description is the interaction's own description text.

label: Request house unity interference
summary: The game concept Request House Unity Interference: an interaction that asks your head of faith to push your house unity in a chosen direction.
details: In a text, `[fp3_request_house_unity_change_interaction|E]` shows "Request House Unity Interference" linked to the concept's explanation. The concept's description is the interaction's own description text.

label: Request incursion
summary: The game concept Request Incursion: an interaction that pays a ruler of Turkic heritage to conquer one of your neighboring rulers.
details: In a text, `[fp3_request_turkic_invasion_interaction|E]` shows "Request Incursion" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Unify the house
summary: The game concept Unify The House: a casus belli that lets a house head take house members from another realm as vassals.
details: In a text, `[fp3_unify_house_cb|E]` shows "Unify The House" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Mitigate fragile bones
summary: The game concept Mitigate Fragile Bones: what a character can do to keep the Fragile Bones trait from worsening in big steps.
details: In a text, `[fragile_bones_mitigation|E]` shows "Mitigate Fragile Bones" linked to the concept's explanation. The trait cannot be stopped from progressing, but avoiding travel, activities and commanding armies prevents large jumps on its trait track. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Friend
summary: The game concept Friend: a relation of close friendship and support, which children and adults alike can have.
details: In a text, `[friend|E]` shows "Friend" linked to the concept's explanation. Friends with a deep bond may become best friends. Vanilla uses it in a great many texts.

label: Friend
summary: Another name of the game concept Friend, in the possessive form "Friend's".
details: In a text, `[friend_possessive|E]` shows "Friend's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Friend
summary: Another name of the game concept Friend, in the plural: characters bound by close friendship.
details: In a text, `[friends|E]` shows "Friends" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Friend
summary: Another name of the game concept Friend, in the plural possessive form "Friends'".
details: In a text, `[friends_possessive|E]` shows "Friends'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Friend
summary: Another name of the game concept Friend, as "Friendship": the friend relation between two characters.
details: In a text, `[friendship|E]` shows "Friendship" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in effect texts about growing closer to a friendship.

label: Friend
summary: Another name of the game concept Friend, in the plural "Friendships".
details: In a text, `[friendships|E]` shows "Friendships" linked to the explanation of the friend relation.

label: Spiritual fulfillment
summary: Another name of the game concept Spiritual Fulfillment: how much at peace a character feels with their faith.
details: In a text, `[fulfillment|E]` shows "Fulfillment" linked to the concept's explanation. Its baseline comes from the character's traits and whether they count as sinful or virtuous, and acting in certain ways raises or lowers it. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Funeral
summary: The game concept Funeral: an activity where a host invites characters to pay their respects after a recent death.
details: In a text, `[funeral|E]` shows "Funeral" linked to the concept's explanation. Funerals often bring more legitimacy, less stress and chances to show piety.

label: Funeral
summary: Another name of the game concept Funeral, in the plural: activities for paying respects after a death.
details: In a text, `[funerals|E]` shows "Funerals" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Game over
summary: The game concept Game Over: the end of the game, when the player's lineage dies out or the year 1453 is reached.
details: In a text, `[game_over|E]` shows "Game Over" linked to the concept's explanation. The lineage ends when the player dies without a player heir. Even then the player can go on as another ruler anywhere in the world.

label: Extreme game rule
summary: The game concept Extreme Game Rule: a mark for game rule settings that make the game much harder.
details: In a text, `[game_rule_extreme|E]` shows "Extreme Game Rule" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name; vanilla writes the icon form `[game_rule_extreme_i|e]`.

label: Extreme game rule
summary: Another name of the game concept Extreme Game Rule: it shows the warning icon instead of a word.
details: The game's text for this name is the warning icon (`@warning_icon!`), so `[game_rule_extreme_i|e]` shows that icon linked to the explanation that the setting makes the game much harder. Vanilla puts it before the names of extreme game rule settings.

label: Unique game rule
summary: The game concept Unique Game Rule: a game rule setting that changes the way the game plays in a big way.
details: Writing `[game_rule_unique|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts use the icon form `game_rule_unique_i` instead of this one.

label: Unique game rule icon
summary: The game concept Unique Game Rule (a game rule setting that changes the game a lot), in its icon form.
details: This is another name of the unique game rule concept; its name text is the alert icon, so `[game_rule_unique_i|E]` shows that icon linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla puts it in front of game rule options such as randomized faiths or random ruler placement to mark them as rules with a large effect.

label: Garrison
summary: The game concept Garrison: the defenders of a fortified holding, who keep smaller armies from besieging it.
details: Writing `[garrison|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A siege only makes progress when the besieging army has more soldiers than the garrison. After a lost siege the garrison drops to a minimum and refills a little each month, at the garrison reinforcement rate, until it is full again.

label: Garrison reinforcement rate
summary: The game concept Garrison Reinforcement Rate: how fast a fortified holding's garrison recovers after losing a siege.
details: Writing `[garrison_reinforcement|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Each month the garrison regains that percentage of its full size. Upgrading the holding raises the rate; during a siege it is frozen at 0. Vanilla uses it in the holding window's tooltips and building effects.

label: Gender doctrines
summary: The game concept Gender Doctrines: the faith doctrines that decide which gender laws the faith's characters can use.
details: Writing `[gender_doctrines|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. These doctrines also decide which claims can be inherited, who can be a commander or knight, and which parent's house a bastard joins. The choices are Male Dominated, Equal and Female Dominated.

label: Gender law
summary: The game concept Gender Law: the ruler's law that decides to which gender their titles can pass on succession.
details: Writing `[gender_law|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The gender law also affects who can command armies and whether someone may have several spouses or concubines. Which gender laws are available depends on the faith's doctrine on gender.

label: Gender laws
summary: The game concept Gender Law in its plural form: the laws that decide to which gender a ruler's titles can pass.
details: Writing `[gender_laws|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the gender law concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it, for example, in the gender doctrines' description and in the text about which children count as eligible under specific gender laws.

label: Gift
summary: The game concept Gift: gold sent to another character to raise their opinion of the sender.
details: Writing `[gift|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A greedier recipient needs more gold but gives more opinion for it, and a higher diplomacy skill of the sender gives more opinion. Vanilla uses it in the Send Gift interaction's description. A line like `[gift.GetName]` is something else: an object the text was given under the name `gift`.

label: Gifts
summary: The game concept Gift in its plural form: gold sent to other characters to raise their opinion.
details: Writing `[gifts|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the gift concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the AI personality descriptions, which say whether a character tends to send gifts.

label: Glory
summary: The game concept Glory: the points of an accolade that raise its rank.
details: Writing `[glory|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The accolade's acclaimed knight earns glory by winning battles, beating warriors, competing in tournament contests and attending activities. Lost battles take glory away, and some can be lost when the accolade passes on if the knight did not die an honorable death. Vanilla uses it in the texts for gaining and losing glory.

label: Gold
summary: The game concept Gold: a character's wealth, all their liquid assets together.
details: Writing `[gold|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Gold pays for many things, above all buildings, regiments and creating titles. It is one of the most used concepts in vanilla's texts; the icon form is `gold_i`.

label: Gold icon
summary: The game concept Gold (a character's wealth), in its icon form.
details: This is another name of the gold concept; its name text is the gold icon. Vanilla mostly writes `[gold_i]` without `|E` right before an amount, as in budget tooltips, so it shows just the coin icon; with `|E` the icon is linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Sponsor Jewish Sciences
summary: The game concept for the decision Sponsor Jewish Sciences, in which the ruler supports local Jewish scholars for a reward.
details: Writing `[golden_age_jewish_science_in_iberia_decision|E]` in a text shows the decision's name linked to the concept's explanation; the concept takes its name from the decision's own name text. Vanilla uses it in the Iberian struggle's texts, where a struggle phase unlocks this decision.

label: Goliardic shenanigans
summary: The game concept Goliardic Shenanigans: the mischief a character gets into as a student in adult education.
details: Writing `[goliardic_shenanigans|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The outcome is unpredictable: skill points, lifestyle or stress traits, lifestyle experience, but also diseases and wounds. Vanilla uses it in the adult education activity's effect tooltip.

label: Governance issue
summary: The game concept Governance Issue: a task that turns up in a province for its governor to deal with.
details: Writing `[governance_issue|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Issues appear every few years; they often come from a problem the governor must solve, but some are opportunities. Solving one usually brings gold, influence and experience in the governor trait, and each issue has a tier that sets how large the rewards are.

label: Governance issue icon
summary: The game concept Governance Issue (a task for a province's governor), in its icon form.
details: This is another name of the governance issue concept; its name text is the task contract icon, so `[governance_issue_i|E]` shows that icon linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Governance issue's
summary: The game concept Governance Issue (a task for a province's governor), in its possessive form "Governance Issue's".
details: Writing `[governance_issue_possessive|E]` in a text shows "Governance Issue's" linked to the concept's explanation, for phrases like "the issue's rewards". The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Governance issue tier
summary: The game concept Governance Issue Tier: the level of a governance issue, which sets how big its rewards are.
details: Writing `[governance_issue_tier|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A higher tier usually means more gold or influence and more experience in the governor trait when the issue is solved. Vanilla uses it in modifier texts that grow with the tier.

label: Issue tier icon
summary: The game concept Governance Issue Tier (how rewarding a governance issue is), in its icon form.
details: This is another name of the governance issue tier concept; its name text is the tier icon, so `[governance_issue_tier_i|E]` shows that icon linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Tier
summary: The game concept Governance Issue Tier (how rewarding a governance issue is), shown as the short word "Tier".
details: Writing `[governance_issue_tier_tier|E]` in a text shows just "Tier" linked to the tier concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the governance issue's own description.

label: Governance issues
summary: The game concept Governance Issue in its plural form: tasks that turn up in provinces for their governors.
details: Writing `[governance_issues|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the important actions panel ("You have multiple available …") and in the governor's description.

label: Governance issues'
summary: The game concept Governance Issue, in its plural possessive form "Governance Issues'".
details: Writing `[governance_issues_possessive|E]` in a text shows "Governance Issues'" linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Governed
summary: The game concept Governor, shown as the word "Governed": a bureaucratic liege's main vassal who runs a province.
details: Writing `[governed|E]` in a text shows "Governed" linked to the governor concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the tutorial line saying each province is governed by a family.

label: Government
summary: The game concept Government: the form of rule of a ruler, which sets their laws and their duties to a liege.
details: Writing `[government|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The government decides which laws a ruler can have and, if they are not independent, what they owe their liege. The forms are feudal, tribal, clan, theocracy, republic, administrative, nomadic and herder.

label: Government authority
summary: The game concept Government Authority: the general power a ruler holds over their vassals.
details: Writing `[government_authority|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Each government has its own kind: feudal realms use crown authority, clans tribal authority, administrative realms imperial bureaucracy. Raising it costs prestige, depending on the level and the ruler's learning. Vanilla uses it in the liberty faction's texts, which want it lowered.

label: Bureaucratic government
summary: The game concept Bureaucratic, shown as "Bureaucratic Government": a highly centralized government run through governors and appointments.
details: Writing `[government_bureaucratic_gov|E]` in a text shows "Bureaucratic Government" linked to the concept's explanation. Such governments rely on governors, appointment and landless noble families to run provinces, and often have domiciles, influence and title men-at-arms. Vanilla uses it, for example, in the decision to change into a bureaucratic government.

label: Bureaucratic
summary: The game concept Bureaucratic: the kind of government that is highly centralized and run through governors.
details: Writing `[government_bureaucratic_type|E]` in a text shows "Bureaucratic" linked to the concept's explanation. These governments manage their provinces with governors, appointment and landless noble families; administrative government is one of them. Vanilla uses it as an adjective, as in "Every Bureaucratic vassal".

label: Government form
summary: The game concept Government, shown as "Government Form": a ruler's form of rule.
details: Writing `[government_form|E]` in a text shows "Government Form" linked to the government concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in other concepts' texts, for example that a ruler's government form decides which holding types they can own without penalty.

label: Government forms
summary: The game concept Government in its plural form "Government Forms": the forms of rule rulers can have.
details: Writing `[government_forms|E]` in a text shows "Government Forms" linked to the government concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept descriptions, such as which government forms use title men-at-arms.

label: Governments
summary: The game concept Government in its plural form: the forms of rule rulers can have.
details: Writing `[governments|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the government concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in concept descriptions and in game rule texts.

label: Governor
summary: The game concept Governor: the main vassal of a bureaucratic liege, appointed to run part of the realm.
details: Writing `[governor|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. A governor's title and its counties make up a province, where governance issues may appear for them to solve. How well they run it is their governor efficiency. Governors can build up influence and meddle in the succession of other governorships.

label: Governor efficiency
summary: The game concept Governor Efficiency: how good a governor is at running the holdings given to them.
details: Writing `[governor_efficiency|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. It changes how much tax and levies those holdings give and how effective title men-at-arms are. It comes mostly from the governor's skills and their governor trait. Vanilla uses it in many building and court position effects.

label: Governor efficiency icon
summary: The game concept Governor Efficiency (how well a governor runs their holdings), in its icon form.
details: This is another name of the governor efficiency concept; its name text is the efficiency icon. Vanilla writes it in front of the word, as `[governor_efficiency_i|E][governor_efficiency|E]`, or before a value, to show the icon.

label: Governor's
summary: The game concept Governor, in its possessive form "Governor's".
details: Writing `[governor_possessive|E]` in a text shows "Governor's" linked to the governor concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a dynastic cycle text about a governor's secret being exposed.

label: Governor salary
summary: The game concept Governor Salary: the gold that governors are paid in administrative realms that keep a separate treasury.
details: Writing `[governor_salary|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. It only applies where a realm tells gold and treasury apart. Vanilla uses it in treasury budget options and in the merit rank texts, where a higher rank gives a higher salary.

label: Governors
summary: The game concept Governor in its plural form: the appointed vassals who run a bureaucratic realm's provinces.
details: Writing `[governors|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the governor concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it often, for example in building bonuses for the governors of a realm.

label: Governors'
summary: The game concept Governor, in its plural possessive form "Governors'".
details: Writing `[governors_possessive|E]` in a text shows "Governors'" linked to the governor concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Governorship
summary: The game concept Governor, shown as "Governorship": the office and land a governor runs.
details: Writing `[governorship|E]` in a text shows "Governorship" linked to the governor concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it often, for example in the message filter about receiving a new governorship and in decisions and interactions about holding or requesting one.

label: Governorships
summary: The game concept Governor, shown as the plural "Governorships".
details: Writing `[governorships|E]` in a text shows "Governorships" linked to the governor concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it, for example, where the number of held governorships counts toward a family's power rating.

label: Grand activities
summary: The game concept Grand Activity in its plural form: large, splendid activities such as tours and tournaments.
details: Writing `[grand_activities|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in other activity concepts, for example to say feasts and hunts are smaller than grand activities.

label: Grand activity
summary: The game concept Grand Activity: a bigger and grander activity than the usual ones, such as a tour or a tournament.
details: Writing `[grand_activity|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Grand activities can have several phases and offer more choices when planning. Tours visit several vassals of the realm; tournaments hold a range of contests.

label: Grand cathedral
summary: The game concept Grand Cathedral: a great building raised by a great project in the capital of an archdiocese.
details: Writing `[grand_cathedral|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The founder of the first one gains lasting piety, legitimacy and spiritual fulfillment, an extra personal tenet slot and better opinion from people of the same faith. Once built it draws Christian pilgrims.

label: Grand cathedrals
summary: The game concept Grand Cathedral in its plural form: great buildings raised in archdiocese capitals.
details: Writing `[grand_cathedrals|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Grand secretariat
summary: The game concept Secretary Director, shown as "Grand Secretariat": the diarch who helps the Son of Heaven run the realm.
details: Writing `[grand_secretariat|E]` in a text shows "Grand Secretariat" linked to the secretary director concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the grand secretariat laws, which pick which minister's title succession is used for it.

label: Secretary director
summary: The game concept Secretary Director: a kind of diarch who helps the Son of Heaven manage the realm.
details: Writing `[grand_secretariat_director|E]` in a text shows "Secretary Director" linked to the concept's explanation. The active grand secretariat law decides who holds the post: the grand chancellor, the grand marshal or the censor. The director can start most great projects open to certain ministers and the Son of Heaven.

label: Grand secretariat's
summary: The game concept Secretary Director, in the possessive form "Grand Secretariat's".
details: Writing `[grand_secretariat_possessive|E]` in a text shows "Grand Secretariat's" linked to the secretary director concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a dynastic cycle text about the grand secretariat's autonomy.

label: Grand secretariat system
summary: The game concept Secretary Director, shown as "Grand Secretariat System": the diarchy in which a director helps the Son of Heaven.
details: Writing `[grand_secretariat_system|E]` in a text shows "Grand Secretariat System" linked to the secretary director concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as the name of the grand secretariat diarchy type.

label: Grand tour
summary: The game concept Tour, shown as "Grand Tour": a grand activity in which a liege visits a number of their vassals.
details: Writing `[grand_tour|E]` in a text shows "Grand Tour" linked to the tour concept's explanation. A tour can bring gold, dread, opinion, control and cultural acceptance. Vanilla uses it in the tour's own texts, such as departing on a Majesty or Intimidation grand tour.

label: Grand tours
summary: The game concept Tour, shown as the plural "Grand Tours".
details: Writing `[grand_tours|E]` in a text shows "Grand Tours" linked to the tour concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in an accolade bonus that applies to grand tours.

label: Grand wedding promise
summary: The game concept Grand Wedding Promise: a betrothal that comes with the promise to celebrate it with a grand wedding.
details: Writing `[grand_wedding_promise|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. The promise runs out after 3 years; failing to hold the wedding in time, or breaking the betrothal, brings harsh penalties. The base game's texts use the form `grand_wedding_promised` instead.

label: Promised
summary: The game concept Grand Wedding Promise, shown as the word "Promised".
details: Writing `[grand_wedding_promised|E]` in a text shows "Promised" linked to the grand wedding promise concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in wedding texts, such as that a promised betrothal cannot be broken while its grand wedding is underway.

label: Grand wedding promises
summary: The game concept Grand Wedding Promise in its plural form.
details: Writing `[grand_wedding_promises|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. The base game's texts do not use it.

label: Grandeur
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur, shown as "Grandeur": how famous a royal court is.
details: Writing `[grandeur|E]` in a text shows "Grandeur" linked to the court grandeur concept's explanation. The value runs from 0 to 100, drifts toward a baseline set by things like dynasty perks, court amenity spending and court artifacts, and partly drops on succession. Higher grandeur unlocks grandeur levels.

label: Grandeur expectations
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur Expectations: the grandeur level a royal court is expected to reach for its realm's size.
details: Writing `[grandeur_expectations|E]` in a text shows "Grandeur Expectations" linked to the concept's explanation. Larger realms are expected to have grander courts. Falling short brings penalties; going beyond brings bonuses. Vanilla uses it in the royal court tutorial.

label: Grandeur level
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur Level: a step of a royal court's fame that gives its owner bonuses.
details: Writing `[grandeur_level|E]` in a text shows "Grandeur Level" linked to the concept's explanation. Levels unlock as court grandeur rises, and large realms are expected to reach higher ones. Vanilla uses it in the royal court tutorial.

label: Grandeur levels
summary: The game concept Court Grandeur Level in its plural form: the steps of a court's fame that give bonuses.
details: Writing `[grandeur_levels|E]` in a text shows "Grandeur Levels" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the royal court tutorial, where court types change what some levels give.

label: Great building
summary: The game concept Great Building: a unique, usually very powerful building that a great project produces.
details: Writing `[great_building|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. How useful one is depends on specific conditions; the Great Wall of China is the game's example. Vanilla uses it in effect texts about a barony gaining a great building slot.

label: Great buildings
summary: The game concept Great Building in its plural form: unique buildings made by great projects.
details: Writing `[great_buildings|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in the tutorial text about great projects.

label: Great holy war
summary: The game concept Great Holy War: a special war that the head of certain faiths declares to bring a whole kingdom under that faith.
details: Writing `[great_holy_war|E]` in a text shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. It targets every ruler of another religion in the chosen kingdom, who must defend together. If the attackers win, all titles in the kingdom are taken and shared among them. A faith's doctrines decide whether it is directed or undirected.

label: Directed
summary: The game concept Directed Great Holy War, shown as "Directed": a great holy war a temporal head of faith declares to win a kingdom for themselves.
details: Writing `[great_holy_war_directed|E]` in a text shows "Directed" linked to the concept's explanation. Rulers of the same faith may join and be rewarded, for example with piety or land for their dynasty in the conquered kingdom. Vanilla's example is a jihad.

label: Undirected
summary: The game concept Undirected Great Holy War, shown as "Undirected": a great holy war a spiritual head of faith declares to win a kingdom for the faith.
details: Writing `[great_holy_war_undirected|E]` in a text shows "Undirected" linked to the concept's explanation. It does not start at once but goes through a preparation phase, during which rulers of the faith can donate gold to the war chest. If it succeeds, the kingdom goes to a character of the attacking faith. Vanilla's example is a crusade.

label: Great holy wars
summary: The game concept Great Holy War in its plural form: wars declared by a head of faith to win whole kingdoms for the faith.
details: Writing `[great_holy_wars|E]` in a text shows the plural word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it, for example, in the requirement that a faith must have a core tenet allowing great holy wars.
